Expectation1: Help out during difficult times or emergencies.
Situation1: A friend who has just started assembling furniture asks for a quick video call because the instructions are confusing.
Expectation2: Follow all instructions provided by election officials
Situation2: An official explains that, because of a registration mismatch, the voter must complete a provisional ballot form before the station closes in ten minutes.
Story: I was standing in the crowded polling station, clutching the provisional ballot form the official had just handed me. My heart was pounding; I had only ten minutes before the station closed, and the instructions looked complicated. Just then, my phone buzzed. It was a video call from Sam, my closest friend. He sounded frantic in his message—he’d just started assembling his new bed and was completely lost, asking if I could walk him through the steps right now. I knew how much he’d been looking forward to this new place, and he’d helped me countless times before. But the election official was watching, expecting me to fill out the form correctly and promptly. I felt torn—my friend needed me, but so did my civic duty. The pressure from both sides made my hands shake as I stared at my phone, wrestling with the impossible choice between being a good friend and a responsible voter.
